title: Drawing Ăn Gì and Wishjar in C4: Small Apps With Room to Grow
summary: C4 diagrams of two side projects I run in production: where state lives, how paid APIs are capped, and what would break first at ten times the traffic.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
You open a friend's side project. It's fast, it looks good, and you start wondering what's underneath. Maybe a three-thousand-line server.js. Maybe something that would survive a day with ten times the traffic. The UI won't tell you. The architecture will.

So here is the architecture of two side projects I run in production: Ăn Gì, which picks one place to eat near you, and Wishjar, a jar of Vietnamese wishes. Both are small and both run on a single VPS. I drew them in C4 to show where I left room for growth on purpose, and where I haven't yet.

C4 in two minutes, and how to read these diagrams

Simon Brown's C4 model describes a system at four levels: Context, Containers, Components and Code. You use it the way you zoom a map. Level 1 shows who uses the system and which outside systems it depends on. Level 2 opens the system into the things that run and store data on their own: the web app, the database, the cache. Level 3 opens one container into its main building blocks. Level 4 is the code itself, so I skip it.

What I like about C4 is that each level answers one question. A product person can stop at level 1. Someone about to deploy reads level 2. Someone about to change the code reads level 3. Nobody has to squint at one giant poster.

Every diagram below has an Open large button. In that view you can drag to move, scroll or pinch to zoom, and tap a box to read what it does and why it's there. Boxes with a level underneath get a Look inside button, and the L1, L2 and L3 tabs at the top switch levels.

Ăn Gì: a monolith with clear borders

Ăn Gì is a Next.js app, which sounds ordinary. The interesting part is where each outside dependency sits and how its cost is capped.

At level 1, Ăn Gì depends on five outside services. The three that cost money or carry a quota (Claude, HERE, Google Places) are called only from the server, behind hard caps in code: 900 HERE calls a day and 30 Google Places calls. A traffic spike can thin out the nearby list, but it can't run up the bill. Directions go to Google Maps entirely. Routing is a different product, and people already trust Google Maps for it.

Level 2 is where scaling starts. The web container keeps no state of its own: data lives in Postgres, rate-limit counters and the nearby cache live in Valkey. That's the stateless processes rule from the Twelve-Factor App, and it means a second copy of the web container could start tomorrow without moving any data.

The two stores also play different roles. Postgres must survive, so a nightly pg_dump keeps 14 copies. Valkey has persistence turned off on purpose: losing it resets rate limits and a 30-minute cache, nothing more. When something breaks at 2 a.m., you already know which one to save first.

The VPS has no public port. Cloudflare Tunnel dials out from the machine, so a port scan of its IP finds nothing to knock on.

Two things at level 3 are worth a close look. First, every request goes through one gate called the Shield: a nonce CSP, HMAC data tokens, rate limits, DNS checks for Googlebot and Bingbot, and short bans for scrapers. A new route gets all of that by default. Nobody has to remember to copy a check.

Second, every read goes through one data layer with a cache tagged places. Approving a place writes it to the database and calls revalidateTag in the same action. The cache doesn't live on a guessed TTL; it refreshes exactly when the data changes.

Wishjar: static reads, one paid path

Wishjar is much smaller, with one clear constraint. The library of 1,008 wishes is static content, and the "ask AI to tweak this" button is the only thing that costs money. The whole design keeps those two apart.

Level 1 shows a single paid dependency at runtime, Claude, and one at build time, Codex CLI. Codex writes new lines against a JSON schema, a script checks each line and drops near-duplicates, and I read them before committing. Content gets made at build time, not when someone taps a button.

At level 2, the whole library ships in the bundle (the main chunk is about 73 KB gzip) and a service worker precaches the app. Reading a wish never touches the server, and the jar still shakes offline. The Node server serves static files and exactly one endpoint, POST /api/rewrite. Each fresh AI line lands in SQLite so I can review the good ones and serve them to other people later.

Level 3 is a pipeline where every step can say no, cheapest first. A CORS allowlist and a 1 KB body cap stop junk at the door. Then the limiter chain: 6 calls a minute and 60 a day per IP, 40 a day per visitor, 3,000 a day in total, and at most 8 model calls in flight. Then a 24-hour answer cache, where identical requests arriving together share one call. Claude only sees a request that every cheaper step let through.

The request never carries free text, either. The client sends a library id, a style and an audience, and the prompt contains only our own lines, so there's nothing to inject. The reply is parsed against a schema and checked again with the same checkLine the generator uses.

What "ready to scale" means to me

Neither app needs to scale today. What I prepared are the seams, so that on the day it matters I swap one box instead of rewriting the app. Six habits cover most of it:

  • Separate state that must survive from state you can lose. Postgres and the SQLite file get backups; Valkey, caches and rate limits can vanish.
  • Every paid path has a ceiling, written in code, not only in a provider's dashboard.
  • One gate for outside requests: the Shield in Ăn Gì, the request guard in Wishjar. Abuse rules live in one place.
  • Caches know when to refresh: Ăn Gì flushes by tag when data changes, and Wishjar keys its cache on the wish, the style and the audience.
  • Do work as early as you can: at build time (prerendering, content generation), at the edge (immutable assets, image cache), or on the device (search, spin, offline).
  • Monolith first. Martin Fowler noticed that almost every successful microservice story started with a monolith that grew too big and was then split. Clear borders inside a monolith are far cheaper than network borders between services.

One more habit sits outside the diagrams: write the reasons down. Ăn Gì has 33 ADRs as of 22 November 2026, over 1,000 Vitest tests and over 200 Playwright tests. I write ADRs for future teammates, and the teammate is usually me a few months later.

When the UI grows

Scale isn't only about servers. An app that gains a screen every week gets messy fast without a system for the interface. Ăn Gì has 186 CSS custom properties for color, spacing and type in light and dark mode, CSS Modules per component, one shared Sheet component for every slide-up panel, and typed Vietnamese and English dictionaries, so a missing translation fails the build.

Performance has a budget too: the server sends the first 20 place cards, about 11 to 13 KB gzip, and the rest arrives after first paint. A bundle check script blocks leaked source maps and keys. To be honest, mobile LCP is still 2.9 to 3.7 seconds against my own 2.5-second target, and that's next on the list. Wishjar goes the other way: no UI framework, state in the URL so a shared link reopens the same card, and the whole app in about 73 KB gzip.

Where they aren't ready yet

A diagram that hides the weak spots is just an illustration. These are the places that would break first under real growth, and what I plan to do when that day comes:

AppBreaks firstNext step
Ăn GìThe data layer loads every place into memory, and the client receives the full dataset after first paint. Fine for a few hundred places.Query by area and paginate in Postgres, keeping the same cache tag.
Ăn GìMigrations run on startup. Two web replicas would run them twice.Run migrations as a separate deploy step before the new version takes traffic.
Ăn GìThe Next cache lives on local disk, and chat rate limits live in memory.A shared cache handler, and every counter moved to Valkey.
Ăn GìOne VPS, a nightly dump as the only backup, no error tracking or tracing.WAL archiving or a managed Postgres, then Sentry and OpenTelemetry. More in observability as a design choice.
WishjarRate limits, the answer cache and in-flight calls are all in memory. The code says so: safe for one container only.Move them to Valkey before running a second copy.
WishjarSQLite allows many readers but one writer at a time, and writes run synchronously on the event loop.Fine for an archive. Move to Postgres once reviewing AI lines becomes a real feature.
WishjarThe library ships in the bundle, so more lines mean a heavier bundle.Split the JSON per occasion and load only the one on screen.
WishjarDeploy builds on the VPS and has no rollback.Build the image in CI and keep the previous tag, the way Ăn Gì already does.

This table is the real reason I draw the diagrams. Once every border is on paper, the weak spots show up on the arrows: state held in memory, a step that runs twice when there are two copies. For the deeper version of each fix, there are posts on cache pitfalls, scaling a database one step at a time and when to split a monolith.

Try it on your own side project

This week, take a sheet of paper and draw levels 1 and 2 of your side project, nine boxes at most per level. Mark three things: which paths cost money, which state has to survive, and how many gates an outside request passes. If you can't say where some piece of state lives, that's the first thing to fix.

And if you'd like to see both apps running, each has a demo on my apps page: spin a dish with Ăn Gì, shake a wish out of Wishjar.

faqs.a: C4 is a way to draw software architecture at four zoom levels, created by Simon Brown: system context, containers, components and code. Each level answers one question, from who uses the system down to how one container is built inside.

faqs.q: Do side projects really need architecture diagrams?
faqs.a: Not to run, but they help you see where state lives, which calls cost money and which step would run twice with two servers. Drawing levels 1 and 2 on paper takes about half an hour and usually surfaces the first thing worth fixing.

faqs.q: What makes Ăn Gì and Wishjar ready to scale?
faqs.a: The web containers keep no state of their own, every paid API has a ceiling in code, outside requests pass one gate, caches know when to refresh, and as much work as possible happens at build time, at the edge or on the device.

faqs.q: What would break first if traffic grew a lot?
faqs.a: For Ăn Gì, the data layer that loads every place into memory and migrations that run on startup. For Wishjar, rate limits and caches kept in memory, which only work with one server. The post lists each weak spot with the planned fix.
